headline: UK unemployment falls to 4.7% but job vacancies drop below 700,000 for the first time since 2021

terms.meaning: Jobs that employers are currently trying to fill.
Average earnings before bonuses are added.
The share of people who want and are looking for work but do not have a job.

levels.headline: UK unemployment falls to 4.7% but job vacancies drop below 700,000 for the first time since 2021
levels.body:
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said on 20 October that the UK unemployment rate was 4.7% in the three months from June to August 2026. The rate fell both over the year and compared with the previous quarter.
Early estimates put job vacancies at 691,000 for July to September, down 21,000 (2.9%) on the previous quarter. It is the first time the total has been below 700,000 since February to April 2021. The fall came mainly from smaller firms, which have suggested they may not be recruiting because of higher labour costs.
Regular pay growth, which excludes bonuses, was 3.7% in June to August and has been steady for six periods. Public sector regular pay grew 6.3%, against 3.0% in the private sector.
The ONS describes the labour market as broadly flat in 2026. The next release is due on 17 November, and the figures will matter to the Bank of England as it weighs inflation against a cooling jobs market.
levels.why: Jobs and pay figures shape decisions on interest rates and show how secure work feels for households.

levels.headline: Unemployment dips to 4.7% as vacancies fall below 700,000
levels.body:
UK unemployment was 4.7% in the three months to August, according to the Office for National Statistics, lower than a year earlier and lower than the previous quarter.
However, the number of job vacancies fell by 21,000 to 691,000 between July and September. That is the first time it has dropped under 700,000 since early 2021. Most of the decline came from smaller employers, who say higher labour costs make them wary of hiring.
Regular pay, excluding bonuses, grew by 3.7% a year, a rate that has barely moved for six periods. Public sector pay is rising much faster, at 6.3%, than private sector pay, at 3.0%.
The ONS says the labour market has been broadly flat this year. Economists will watch the next figures, due on 17 November, because the Bank of England uses them when deciding whether to change interest rates.
levels.why: A weaker hiring picture could influence how far the Bank of England goes on interest rates.

levels.headline: Unemployment edges down to 4.7% but employers advertise fewer jobs
levels.body:
The share of people in the UK who are out of work fell to 4.7% in the June to August period, official figures show. That is slightly better than both last year and the previous three months.
But employers are advertising fewer jobs. Vacancies dropped by 21,000 to 691,000 in the July to September period, the lowest level since early 2021. The Office for National Statistics says smaller firms are leading the fall and may be holding back because of the cost of employing people.
Wages are still rising by 3.7% a year before bonuses. Public sector workers have seen pay rise by 6.3%, while private sector pay has risen by 3.0%.
Overall, the ONS calls the jobs market broadly flat this year. The next set of figures comes out on 17 November, and the Bank of England will study them closely when it considers interest rates.
levels.why: It suggests the jobs market is steady but not strengthening, which affects pay and prices.

levels.headline: Fewer people are unemployed, but there are fewer jobs on offer too
levels.body:
The unemployment rate in the UK fell to 4.7% in the three months to August. This means that just under five in every hundred people who wanted a job could not find one.
The number of job vacancies, which are jobs employers are trying to fill, also fell. There were 691,000 between July and September, which is 21,000 fewer than the previous three months. The Office for National Statistics said this is the first time the figure has been under 700,000 since 2021. Smaller firms are mostly responsible, partly because of the cost of employing staff.
Pay is rising by 3.7% a year, not counting bonuses. Public sector pay is growing faster, at 6.3%, than pay in private firms, at 3.0%.
The jobs market has been fairly flat all year. The next figures are due on 17 November.
levels.why: Pay and jobs affect how much households can spend and what the Bank of England does next.

levels.headline: UK unemployment falls a little, but fewer jobs are being advertised
levels.body:
New figures show that 4.7% of people in the UK who could work were without a job between June and August. That is a small improvement on last year. The numbers come from the Office for National Statistics, which counts things like jobs and prices for the country.
There is a less cheerful side. Employers are advertising fewer jobs. A job advert is called a vacancy. There were 691,000 vacancies from July to September, which is 21,000 fewer than before. It is the lowest total since 2021. Small firms are leading the drop. They say hiring has become too costly.
Pay is going up by 3.7% a year, before bonuses. Workers in public services such as schools and hospitals saw 6.3%. Private firms paid 3.0%.
The next figures are due on 17 November.
levels.why: Fewer adverts mean people looking for work may find it harder, even though unemployment is lower.

levels.headline: Fewer people are out of work, but there are fewer jobs to apply for
levels.body:
The latest official figures show that 4.7% of people in the UK were out of work between June and August. That is a little lower than a year ago.
But there are fewer jobs on offer. Companies advertised 691,000 jobs between July and September. That is 21,000 fewer than the three months before, and the lowest number since 2021. Smaller firms are hiring less. They say it costs them more to employ people now.
Pay is still going up. Wages grew by 3.7% over the year, not counting bonuses. People who work for the public sector, such as nurses and teachers, saw pay rise by 6.3%. In private firms it was 3.0%.
The Office for National Statistics says the jobs market has not changed much this year. More figures will come on 17 November. Banks and the government will watch them.
levels.why: If hiring slows, it can be harder to find work or to ask for a pay rise.

levels.headline: The number of people without jobs has fallen, but fewer jobs are being offered
levels.body:
Good news first. The share of people without a job fell a little to 4.7%. This is about five in every hundred people who are able to work. The figure covers June to August and comes from the Office for National Statistics, a group that counts things for the country.
Now the less good news. Fewer jobs are being offered. These open jobs are called vacancies. There were 691,000 of them, which is 21,000 fewer than before. It is the lowest number since 2021. Small businesses say that paying staff costs a lot, so they are hiring fewer people.
Pay is still rising by 3.7% a year. Public workers, such as teachers, saw a rise of 6.3%. Workers in private companies saw 3.0%.
New figures come out on 17 November.
levels.why: It shows whether it is easy or hard for people to find work and earn more.

levels.headline: Fewer people are without work, but fewer jobs are on offer
levels.body:
Some people want a job and cannot find one. This week we learned that about five in every hundred workers are in that position. The exact figure is 4.7%. That is a little lower than last year. The numbers come from a group called the ONS, which counts things like jobs and prices.
But there is a worry too. Companies are putting up fewer job adverts. These open jobs are called vacancies. There are 691,000. That is 21,000 fewer than before. It is the lowest since 2021. Small shops and firms say it costs a lot to hire workers.
Pay is still growing. Most workers are paid 3.7% more than a year ago. People who work for the government get 6.3% more. People in private firms get 3.0% more.
We will hear more on 17 November.
levels.why: Jobs help families pay for food, homes and fun things, so it matters when fewer jobs are offered.

levels.headline: Fewer people are out of work, but fewer jobs are being offered
levels.body:
Some grown-ups do not have a job but want one. This week, we learned that this is true for about five in every hundred grown-ups who can work. That is a little better than last year. The numbers come from a group called the ONS, which counts things for the country.
But there is a worry. Shops and firms are asking for fewer new workers. Each empty job is called a vacancy. There are 691,000 of them. That is fewer than before. It is the lowest since 2021. Small firms say it costs a lot to pay workers, so they hire fewer.
Pay is still going up a little. Most workers get 3.7% more than last year.
We will hear more on 17 November.
levels.why: Jobs help families pay for food and homes, so it matters when fewer are offered.

levels.headline: Fewer grown-ups are out of work, but there are fewer new jobs
levels.body:
Think of a town where grown-ups want jobs, such as working in shops, schools or offices. Most have a job. A few do not. This week a group called the ONS counted them. It found that about five in every hundred grown-ups who want to work had no job. That is slightly better than last year.
But shops and firms are asking for fewer new workers. Each empty job they want to fill is called a vacancy. There are 691,000 of them now. That is fewer than before. Small firms say workers cost a lot of money, so they hire fewer.
Pay is still going up a little. Most workers earn a bit more than last year.
We will hear the next news on 17 November.
levels.why: Grown-ups with jobs earn money for food, homes and treats, so it matters when fewer jobs appear.

headline: S&P 500 closes up 0.28% at 7,712.57 as the Dow jumps more than 1% on earnings

terms.meaning: An index tracking the share prices of 500 of the biggest US companies.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, an index of 30 large US companies.
A US stock market, and its index, packed with technology firms.

levels.headline: S&P 500 closes up 0.28% at 7,712.57 as the Dow jumps more than 1% on earnings
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed up on Tuesday 20 October, the last completed trading session, gaining 0.28% to finish at 7,712.57. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 529.85 points, or 1.02%, to 52,495.88. The Nasdaq Composite was almost unchanged, slipping 0.02% to 26,424.82.
CNBC linked the Dow's strength to upbeat company earnings and falling oil prices. Shares in 3M rose more than 5% after it beat forecasts and raised its guidance. Some stocks linked to artificial intelligence recovered later in the session.
The rebound followed a difficult week. The S&P 500 lost nearly 2% in the previous week and the Nasdaq fell 4.5%, amid worries about companies borrowing heavily to build AI capacity.
Opinion is split. Capital Economics expects the S&P 500 to fall to 6,500 by the end of next year, while other firms argue the recent tech selling was overdone.
levels.why: US share prices affect pensions and savings around the world and signal how confident investors feel.

levels.headline: Wall Street ends higher, with the S&P 500 up 0.28% and the Dow up more than 1%
levels.body:
The S&P 500 rose 0.28% to close at 7,712.57 on Tuesday 20 October, the latest completed session. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 529.85 points, or 1.02%, to 52,495.88, while the Nasdaq Composite edged down 0.02% to 26,424.82.
Better-than-expected company results and lower oil prices helped, according to CNBC. Shares in 3M jumped more than 5% after the firm beat expectations and lifted its outlook. Some AI-related shares bounced back during the day.
It came after a rough previous week, when the S&P 500 lost nearly 2% and the Nasdaq dropped 4.5% on concerns about the debt companies are taking on to fund AI projects.
Forecasts differ. Capital Economics thinks the S&P 500 could fall to 6,500 by the end of next year, but some analysts say the recent sell-off in technology went too far.
levels.why: Moves on Wall Street can sway markets worldwide, including the value of UK pension funds.

levels.headline: US shares rise as strong company results lift the Dow by more than 1%
levels.body:
US stocks mostly rose on Tuesday 20 October. The S&P 500, which tracks 500 large American companies, gained 0.28% and closed at 7,712.57. The Dow Jones, which follows 30 big firms, jumped 1.02% to 52,495.88. The Nasdaq, which is full of technology companies, slipped 0.02% to 26,424.82.
CNBC said the gains were helped by strong company profits and falling oil prices. The firm 3M saw its share price rise by more than 5% after reporting results better than expected. Some artificial intelligence companies recovered later in the day.
The previous week was rough. The S&P 500 fell almost 2% and the Nasdaq fell 4.5% as investors worried about firms borrowing a lot to build AI systems.
Analysts disagree about what comes next. One firm expects a big fall, while others think the sell-off went too far.
levels.why: Stock prices show how confident investors are, and they affect savings and pensions.

levels.headline: Wall Street finishes higher, led by a strong day for the Dow
levels.body:
Share prices in the United States mostly went up on Tuesday 20 October. The S&P 500 index, which follows 500 big American companies, rose 0.28% to 7,712.57. The Dow Jones index, which follows 30 large firms, rose 1.02% to 52,495.88. The Nasdaq, which has many technology firms, dipped by 0.02% to 26,424.82.
One reason was that several companies reported profits that were better than people expected. Oil prices also fell, which helps firms that spend a lot on fuel. The company 3M saw its shares rise by over 5%.
The week before was bad for shares. Investors worried that some companies were borrowing too much money to build artificial intelligence, or AI. Share prices of those companies fell.
Some experts think prices may fall further. Others think the fall was too big.
levels.why: When share prices move a lot, it can change the value of people's savings and pensions.

levels.headline: US share prices go up on Tuesday, with the Dow doing best
levels.body:
Share prices in America mostly rose on Tuesday 20 October. A share is a small piece of a company. People buy shares hoping the company will do well.
To see how shares are doing, people watch groups of them called indexes. The S&P 500 follows 500 big companies. It rose 0.28% to 7,712.57. The Dow follows 30 large companies. It rose 1.02% to 52,495.88. The Nasdaq follows many technology companies. It fell a tiny bit, by 0.02%, to 26,424.82.
Companies shared profits that were better than people hoped, and oil got cheaper. The firm 3M saw its shares rise by more than 5%.
The week before was hard. Worries about AI spending made prices drop. Some experts think more falls could come, and others do not.
levels.why: Share prices affect pensions and savings, so they matter to many families.

levels.headline: American share prices rise, led by large companies
levels.body:
On Tuesday 20 October, share prices in America mostly went up. A share is a tiny slice of a company that people can buy. If the company does well, the slice can become worth more.
People follow share prices using lists called indexes. One is the S&P 500, which follows 500 big companies. It went up a little, by 0.28%. Another is the Dow, which follows 30 large companies. It went up by 1.02%. A third is the Nasdaq, which follows many technology companies. It dipped by almost nothing.
The prices went up because many companies said they had earned more money than people guessed. Oil also got cheaper.
The week before, prices fell because people worried about companies spending huge sums on AI computers. Nobody knows what will happen next.
levels.why: Many people's savings are in shares, so rising or falling prices can change how rich or worried they feel.

levels.headline: Shares in America go up on Tuesday
levels.body:
Some companies are so big that you can buy a small piece of them. That piece is called a share. When people think a company will do well, the price of its shares goes up. When they worry, it goes down.
On Tuesday 20 October, many share prices in America went up. To keep track, people use lists called indexes. The S&P 500 list follows 500 big companies. It went up by a small amount. The Dow list follows 30 large companies. It went up by more, about 1%. The Nasdaq list follows technology companies. It stayed almost the same.
Companies said they had earned more than people expected, and oil became cheaper. That made people feel more hopeful.
The week before had been scary, and prices had dropped.
levels.why: Lots of families save money in shares, so it matters when prices go up or down.

levels.headline: Shares in America had a good Tuesday
levels.body:
A share is like a tiny slice of a company. If you own a slice of a bakery and the bakery sells lots of cakes, your slice becomes worth more. If it sells fewer cakes, your slice becomes worth less.
On Tuesday, many slices of big American companies became worth a little more. People keep track using lists called indexes. One list follows 500 big companies. It went up a little. Another list follows 30 big companies. It went up by about one in every hundred. A third list, full of technology firms, stayed about the same.
Many companies said they had sold more than people guessed. That made people feel hopeful.
The week before, prices had gone down, so some people are still a bit nervous.
levels.why: Grown-ups often keep savings in shares, so rising prices can help families feel safe.

levels.headline: Shares in America go up a little on Tuesday
levels.body:
A share is a tiny piece of a company. People buy shares and hope the company does well. Then the piece is worth more.
On Tuesday, many shares in America went up. People keep track using lists called indexes. One list follows 500 big companies. It went up a little. Another list follows 30 big companies. It went up by about one in every hundred. A list of technology companies stayed almost the same.
Many companies said they had earned more money than people had guessed. Oil also got cheaper. That made people feel more hopeful.
The week before was a bad one, and prices fell. Some experts think they may fall again. Others think they will not.
levels.why: Many people keep savings in shares, so rising or falling prices matter to families.

levels.headline: Wall Street has a good day after a bad week
levels.body:
Imagine the playground swap-card market. When lots of children want a card, its price goes up. When they get worried, the price falls. Shares work in a similar way, but they are tiny pieces of real companies.
On Tuesday, many shares in America became worth a bit more. Grown-ups follow lists of shares called indexes. One list of 500 big companies went up a little. Another list of 30 big companies went up by about one in a hundred. A list of technology companies stayed about the same.
The reason was that many companies said they had done better than people thought.
The week before had been a bad one, so this was a happier day.
levels.why: Many families keep savings in shares, so happy or sad days in the market can touch everyone.

headline: Burnham weighs closer EU ties as a senior MEP floats a 'Switzerland plus' deal

terms.meaning: A possible UK deal modelled on Switzerland's close but partial links with the EU, with extra areas added.
The EU trading area where goods and services move freely under common rules.
The way things are now, with no change.

levels.headline: Burnham weighs closer EU ties as a senior MEP floats a 'Switzerland plus' deal
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is pushing for closer ties with the European Union, and a senior MEP has said a 'Switzerland plus' deal is one option. Bernd Lange said such an arrangement could cover political cooperation as well as trade, security, raw materials and digital policy, and could be negotiated within months of a decision to deepen relations.
The Swiss model involves partial single market access, a payment into the EU's cohesion fund and free movement of people.
Mr Burnham has listed options including keeping things as they are, a customs union, the single market, or going all the way and rejoining. He says the status quo is not good enough. In his Commons statement on 12 October he said the immediate priority was a successful UK-EU summit, followed by serious talks on the long-term options. He has not ruled out a referendum but says it would not be right now.
levels.why: The shape of Britain's future relationship with the EU affects trade, prices, jobs and travel.

levels.headline: Burnham sets out options for closer EU ties, and an MEP suggests 'Switzerland plus'
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham wants a closer relationship with the EU, and German MEP Bernd Lange says a 'Switzerland plus' deal is one way to get there. He said it could include political cooperation, trade, security, raw materials and digital policy, and could be agreed within months once Britain decides to go ahead.
Switzerland has partial access to the EU single market. It pays into an EU fund for poorer regions and accepts free movement of people.
Mr Burnham has outlined choices: stay as things are, join a customs union, join the single market, or rejoin fully. He has said staying as things are is not good enough. He told MPs on 12 October that the first task is a successful UK-EU summit, then a serious debate on the longer term. A referendum is not ruled out, but he says now is not the time.
levels.why: It could decide how easily goods, workers and travellers move between Britain and Europe.

levels.headline: A 'Switzerland plus' deal is floated as Burnham looks for closer EU links
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham wants Britain to work more closely with the European Union. A senior member of the European Parliament, Bernd Lange, says one choice is a 'Switzerland plus' deal. It would go further than the arrangement Switzerland has. It could cover politics, trade, security and digital rules, and he thinks it could be agreed in a few months if Britain decides to go ahead.
Switzerland takes part in parts of the EU's single market, pays money to the EU and allows people from EU countries to live and work there freely.
Mr Burnham has listed several routes, from keeping things as they are to rejoining the EU. He says doing nothing is not good enough. He told MPs the first step is a UK-EU summit. He has not ruled out a vote on rejoining, but not yet.
levels.why: Closer EU links could change what Britain pays, sells and who can work here.

levels.headline: Burnham wants a closer relationship with the EU, and one option is 'Switzerland plus'
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says Britain should have a closer relationship with the European Union. A senior EU politician, Bernd Lange, has said one idea is a 'Switzerland plus' deal. This would copy some of how Switzerland works with the EU, and add more, such as cooperation on security and digital rules. He thinks it could be agreed within months.
Switzerland can trade with the EU more easily than most countries. In return, it pays money to the EU and lets EU citizens live and work there.
Mr Burnham says there are several choices. Britain could stay as it is, or get closer, or even rejoin the EU. He says staying as it is would not be good enough. He wants a UK-EU summit to go well first. A new vote on rejoining is not ruled out, but is not planned now.
levels.why: The choice affects trade, prices and whether people can live and work abroad.

levels.headline: Britain looks at getting closer to the EU, and 'Switzerland plus' is one idea
levels.body:
Britain left the European Union in 2020. Now Prime Minister Andy Burnham wants the two to work together more closely. A leading EU politician, Bernd Lange, says one idea is called 'Switzerland plus'.
Switzerland is not in the EU, but it has a deal that lets it trade with the EU easily. In return it pays some money to the EU and lets EU citizens live and work there. 'Plus' means Britain could add more, such as working together on safety and on the rules for the internet. Mr Lange thinks a deal could be ready in a few months if Britain wanted one.
Mr Burnham says there are many choices, from changing little to rejoining the EU. He says changing nothing is not good enough. First he wants a summit with the EU to go well. A vote on rejoining is not planned yet.
levels.why: Deals with Europe affect what things cost in shops and how easily people can work or travel there.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister wants closer links with the EU, and a new kind of deal is suggested
levels.body:
Britain used to be in the European Union, a group of countries that work and trade together. It left in 2020. Now Prime Minister Andy Burnham says the UK should get closer to the EU again.
An EU politician named Bernd Lange has an idea called 'Switzerland plus'. Switzerland is not in the EU. But it has a deal that lets it sell goods to EU countries easily. In return it pays money and lets EU citizens live and work there. 'Plus' means Britain could add more, such as working together on safety.
Mr Burnham says Britain could do nothing new, get a little closer, or even rejoin. He says doing nothing is not good enough. A meeting with the EU comes first. A new public vote is not planned yet.
levels.why: A closer deal could change prices, jobs and travel for ordinary people.

levels.headline: Britain may get closer to Europe
levels.body:
Britain used to belong to the European Union, which is a club of countries that trade and work together. Britain left in 2020. Now the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, says it should get closer to the club again.
An important EU politician has an idea. He calls it 'Switzerland plus'. Switzerland is a country that is not in the club, but it has a special deal. It can sell things to the club easily. In return, it pays some money and lets people from the club live and work there. 'Plus' means Britain could add more, such as teaming up on safety.
The Prime Minister says there are many choices. Doing nothing is not good enough, he says. First there will be a big meeting with the EU.
levels.why: The choice could change what things cost and where people can work.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister wants Britain to be better friends with Europe
levels.body:
Imagine Britain used to be in a club with many other countries. Then Britain left. Now the leader, the Prime Minister Andy Burnham, wants to be closer friends with the club again.
An important person from the club has a new idea. It is like the deal that a country called Switzerland has. Switzerland is not in the club, but it has special rules that make trading easy. In return, it pays some money and lets club members live there. 'Plus' means Britain could do even more together, like helping to keep everyone safe.
The Prime Minister says there are many choices. He says doing nothing is not good enough. First, there will be a big meeting.
levels.why: It matters because it could change what shops sell, what things cost and who can work where.

levels.headline: Britain may become closer friends with Europe
levels.body:
Britain used to be in the European Union. That is a club of countries that trade and work together. Britain left in 2020. Now the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, says Britain should get closer to the club again.
An important person from the club has an idea. It is called 'Switzerland plus'. Switzerland is a country that is not in the club, but it has a special deal. It can sell things to the club easily. It pays some money and lets people from the club live there. 'Plus' means Britain could do even more together, such as keeping each other safe.
The Prime Minister says doing nothing is not good enough. First there is a big meeting. Then more talks.
levels.why: A deal could change what things cost and where people can work.

levels.headline: Britain thinks about being closer friends with its neighbours
levels.body:
Think of countries as schools in the same area. Britain used to be in a team with its neighbours, but it left the team. Now the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, wants to work together with them more.
Someone important from the team has a plan. It is like how another country, Switzerland, works with the team. Switzerland is not on the team, but it shares some rules so it can swap goods easily. In return, it gives some money. 'Plus' means Britain could share even more, like helping each other stay safe.
The Prime Minister says doing nothing is not good enough. First there will be a big meeting to talk about it. Nobody has decided yet.
levels.why: Friendly deals with neighbours can change what things cost and where people can work.

headline: Markets expect a Bank of England rate rise as gilt yields stay high before the 28 October Budget

terms.meaning: The Bank of England's main interest rate, which influences loan and savings rates.
A bond issued by the UK government to borrow money.
The return investors get on a bond, which rises when its price falls.

levels.headline: Markets expect a Bank of England rate rise as gilt yields stay high before the 28 October Budget
levels.body:
The Bank of England's Bank Rate stands at 3.75%, but markets increasingly expect a rise. At its meeting on 16 September, the Monetary Policy Committee voted 6 to 3 to hold, with three members preferring a quarter-point increase to 4%. One report says markets now price a near 80% chance of a 25 basis point rise in November, although bets on a 5 November increase have eased slightly.
UK inflation rose to 3.1% in August from 2.9% in July, with motor fuel costs a major factor and energy prices linked to the Middle East conflict the main driver. September's figure is due on 21 October.
Gilt yields remain elevated. Trading Economics put the 10-year yield at about 5.44% on 20 October, though its reports show different levels on different days. The Budget is on 28 October, and higher borrowing costs are reducing the government's room for manoeuvre and raising expectations of tax rises.
levels.why: Interest rates and government borrowing costs shape mortgages, savings and taxes.

levels.headline: Rate rise bets and high gilt yields put pressure on the Chancellor before the Budget
levels.body:
The Bank of England's main interest rate, Bank Rate, is 3.75%. On 16 September the Bank's rate-setters voted 6 to 3 to leave it unchanged, with three wanting a rise to 4%. Reports say investors now see a near 80% chance of a quarter-point rise in November, though some bets on 5 November have eased.
Inflation rose to 3.1% in August from 2.9% in July. Higher fuel costs are a big part of this, linked to energy prices and the conflict in the Middle East. The September figure is due on 21 October.
Gilts, the bonds the government sells to borrow money, are paying high returns. The 10-year yield was about 5.44% on 20 October. This makes borrowing dearer for the government, reduces its spare room in the budget and raises expectations of tax increases when the Chancellor, John Healey, speaks on 28 October.
levels.why: It affects the cost of mortgages and whether taxes rise in the Budget.

levels.headline: Investors expect interest rates to rise again as the Budget nears
levels.body:
The Bank of England's interest rate is 3.75%. In September, the group that sets it voted 6 to 3 to keep it there. Three members wanted to raise it to 4%. Now investors think a rise in November is very likely, with one report putting the chance at nearly 80%.
The reason is inflation, which is the rate at which prices rise. It went up to 3.1% in August from 2.9% in July, mostly because of fuel costs linked to the conflict in the Middle East. New figures are due on 21 October.
The government also pays more to borrow. Gilts are the bonds it sells to raise money, and their yields, or returns for investors, are high. The 10-year yield was about 5.44% on 20 October. With the Budget on 28 October, many expect tax rises.
levels.why: Higher rates can mean dearer mortgages and loans, while tax decisions affect everyone's pay packets.

levels.headline: Interest rates may go up again, and the government is paying more to borrow
levels.body:
The Bank of England sets an interest rate that affects what people pay on loans and mortgages. It is now 3.75%. In September, the Bank's committee voted 6 to 3 to leave it alone. Three members wanted to increase it to 4%. Many investors now think a rise will come in November.
The worry is inflation, which means prices going up. It rose to 3.1% in August, partly because petrol and energy cost more due to trouble in the Middle East. The newest figure is due on 21 October.
The government also borrows money by selling bonds called gilts. Right now it has to offer high returns to investors, around 5.44% for 10-year gilts. That leaves less money to spend. The Chancellor, John Healey, will give a Budget on 28 October, and many expect tax rises.
levels.why: Higher borrowing costs for the government can lead to higher taxes or less spending.

levels.headline: Interest rates may rise again, and borrowing is getting more costly for the government
levels.body:
The Bank of England is the bank that looks after Britain's money. It sets an interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. It is 3.75% now. In September, a group at the Bank voted on whether to raise it. Six said no. Three said yes. Many people who invest money now think the Bank will raise it in November.
The reason is that prices are rising faster. This is called inflation. It went up to 3.1% in August. Petrol and energy cost more because of fighting in the Middle East.
The government borrows too, by selling bonds called gilts. To get people to buy them, it must pay about 5.4% a year on the 10-year ones. That is a lot. The Chancellor, John Healey, will announce the Budget on 28 October. Many people expect higher taxes.
levels.why: If borrowing costs more, mortgages and taxes can both feel the squeeze.

headline: Brent crude hits a five-month high near $111 as attacks on ships and Saudi sites fuel supply worries

terms.meaning: The main international price for a barrel of oil.
A narrow sea route in the Gulf through which much of the world's oil ships pass.
How much of something, such as oil, is available to buy.

levels.headline: Brent crude hits a five-month high near $111 as attacks on ships and Saudi sites fuel supply worries
levels.body:
Brent crude futures rose to $111.05 a barrel on 20 October, the highest since May, before easing. Trading Economics put the price at about $109.29 later that day, down 0.24% on the previous session. Brent is up about 8.9% over the past month and 78% on a year ago.
CNBC links the rise to Iranian attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi strikes on Saudi infrastructure. One report said Brent fell about 1% to nearly $108 after an unconfirmed claim that Qatar and Pakistan had presented a new proposal to revive talks to end the Iran war.
Trading Economics' own model expects Brent near $113.86 by the end of the quarter, though that is a model estimate, not a market consensus.
Higher oil prices feed through to petrol, heating and transport costs, and they are a main reason inflation has been rising in the UK and elsewhere.
levels.why: Oil prices drive petrol bills, transport costs and inflation for households and firms.

levels.headline: Oil reaches its highest level since May as Middle East attacks threaten supply
levels.body:
Brent crude, the global benchmark, touched $111.05 a barrel on 20 October, its highest since May, then eased to about $109. It is up almost 9% in a month and about 78% in a year.
The rise reflects attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz by Iran and strikes on Saudi infrastructure by the Houthis, which worry traders about supply. Prices slipped about 1% towards $108 at one point after an unconfirmed report that Qatar and Pakistan had put forward a fresh proposal to restart talks to end the Iran war.
Trading Economics' model sees Brent near $113.86 by the end of the quarter, but that is an estimate rather than a market consensus.
Expensive oil pushes up fuel and transport costs and is one of the main reasons that inflation has risen recently in Britain and other countries.
levels.why: Dearer oil raises the cost of petrol, travel and many goods.

levels.headline: Oil prices hit a five-month high because of attacks in the Middle East
levels.body:
The price of Brent crude, the main international measure of oil, rose as high as $111.05 a barrel on 20 October. That is the highest since May. By the end of the day it was around $109. The price has gone up by almost 9% in a month and by about 78% in a year.
The main cause is worry about supply. Iran has attacked tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route that carries much of the world's oil. The Houthis, an Iran-backed group, have hit Saudi sites. Prices dipped at one point after an unconfirmed report of a new plan from Qatar and Pakistan to restart peace talks.
A forecasting model expects around $114 by the end of the quarter, but that is only an estimate.
Higher oil prices push up the cost of fuel and transport.
levels.why: It can make petrol, bills and shop prices rise.

levels.headline: Oil is at its most expensive since May because of trouble in the Middle East
levels.body:
The price of oil is climbing. Brent crude, the main global price, reached $111.05 a barrel on 20 October. That is the highest since May. It then fell back to about $109. In one month it has risen almost 9%. In one year it has risen about 78%.
The cause is worry that there will not be enough oil. Iran has attacked tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route that many oil ships use. A group called the Houthis has attacked places in Saudi Arabia. The price dipped for a while when a report said Qatar and Pakistan had a new peace plan, but this was not confirmed.
When oil costs more, petrol, travel and heating can cost more too. This is one reason prices have been rising.
levels.why: Oil costs touch almost everything, from petrol to the price of food in shops.

levels.headline: Oil costs more because ships and oil sites in the Middle East have been attacked
levels.body:
Oil is a thick liquid that is turned into petrol and diesel. It is sold by the barrel. The main world price is called Brent crude. On 20 October it reached $111.05 a barrel. That is the highest since May. It later fell to about $109. A year ago it cost much less. It has risen by about 78%.
The price goes up when people worry there will not be enough oil. Iran has attacked ships in a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz, where many oil ships go. A group called the Houthis has attacked places in Saudi Arabia. A report said Qatar and Pakistan have a new peace plan, but no one has confirmed it.
Expensive oil makes petrol and heating cost more.
levels.why: When oil costs more, many other things in the shops cost more too.

levels.headline: The price of oil has jumped because of fighting in the Middle East
levels.body:
Oil is dug from the ground and made into petrol for cars and fuel for planes. The main world price is called Brent. On 20 October it hit $111 for each barrel. It had not been that high since May. It is up about 78% on a year ago.
The price jumps when people think there may not be enough oil. Iran has attacked ships on a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz, which many oil ships use. A group called the Houthis has attacked places in Saudi Arabia. A report said two countries, Qatar and Pakistan, had a new plan for peace. No one has confirmed it.
When oil costs more, petrol and heating can cost more, and so can food.
levels.why: It affects the price of petrol, travel and the things in shops.

levels.headline: Oil is getting much more expensive
levels.body:
Oil is a liquid from deep under the ground. We turn it into petrol and diesel for cars and lorries. Oil is sold in barrels, and a barrel now costs about $109. That is much more than last year.
Why? Because there is fighting in the Middle East. Ships carrying oil have been attacked in a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. Places that make oil in Saudi Arabia have been attacked too. When people worry there will not be enough oil, they are ready to pay more for it.
Some people say there could be a new peace plan, but no one has said it is real yet.
When oil costs more, petrol costs more, and so does the cost of moving food to the shops.
levels.why: It can make petrol and shopping cost more for families.

levels.headline: Oil costs a lot more because of fighting far away
levels.body:
Oil is a thick black liquid from under the ground. It is turned into petrol for cars and buses. A barrel of it is a big container. A barrel now costs about $109. A year ago it cost much less.
Why is it so expensive? There is fighting in the Middle East. Ships carrying oil have been attacked. Oil sites in a country called Saudi Arabia have been attacked too. When people fear there may not be enough oil, they will pay more to get it. It is like when the last ice lolly in the shop costs extra because everybody wants it.
Some grown-ups hope for a peace plan, but it is not certain.
Expensive oil can make petrol and food cost more.
levels.why: It can make the things families buy cost more.

levels.headline: A war at sea in the Middle East
levels.body:
There is a war in the Middle East. This week, ships that carry oil were attacked at sea. Nine ships have been hit since Sunday. Oil is used to make petrol, so these ships matter to lots of people.
One country, Iran, wants to stop the ships passing through a narrow stretch of sea. It says it will let them through only if the United States agrees to seven things. A group called the Houthis, who back Iran, has also fired rockets at Saudi Arabia, a country with lots of oil.
A small country called Qatar is helping the two sides talk. So far, there is no deal.
Everyone hopes for peace.
levels.why: Ships carry oil to many countries, so fighting at sea can make fuel cost more.

levels.headline: Why petrol could cost more
levels.body:
Cars and buses need petrol to move. Petrol is made from oil, a thick black liquid found deep underground. Oil is kept in big barrels, and the price of a barrel has gone up a lot. It costs about $109 now. A year ago it cost much less.
Why? There is fighting far away in the Middle East. Ships that carry oil have been attacked, and so have places that make oil. When people worry there will not be enough, they will pay more. It is like when everyone in the playground wants the same toy and the owner asks for more.
Grown-ups are hoping for peace, but they are not sure.
When oil costs more, petrol and food can cost more too.
levels.why: It can make everyday things cost more for families.

headline: Tanker attacks in the Gulf and Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia deepen the Iran war as mediators seek a deal

terms.meaning: Iran's powerful military force, also called the IRGC.
An Iran-backed armed group in Yemen.
Stopping ships or goods from entering or leaving a place.

levels.headline: Tanker attacks in the Gulf and Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia deepen the Iran war as mediators seek a deal
levels.body:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said naval mines stopped three tankers using routes Tehran considers unauthorised, and two were set ablaze. At least nine tankers and cargo ships have come under attack since Sunday, as Iran tries to choke oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's foreign ministry has warned Washington it would retaliate against any strike.
Tehran says the strait will not reopen until seven conditions based on the Islamabad Memorandum are met, including an end to US 'acts of aggression', the lifting of the US naval blockade and the release of Iranian assets.
Separately, the Iran-allied Houthis have repeatedly fired at Saudi Arabia this week. Saudi forces intercepted missiles, including one aimed at the Yanbu export terminal, and an Aramco administrative building in Dhahran was hit on Tuesday. The Houthis have also declared a maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia.
Qatar is acting as a back channel and its prime minister has visited Tehran. Earlier, Qatar and Pakistan presented a proposal for a 10-day ceasefire.
levels.why: The war threatens oil supplies and prices worldwide, and any ceasefire would affect everyone's energy bills.

levels.headline: Iran and the Houthis escalate attacks on shipping and Saudi sites as talks stall
levels.body:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said mines stopped three tankers on routes Tehran does not authorise, and two caught fire. At least nine tankers and cargo ships have been attacked since Sunday as Iran tries to squeeze oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's foreign ministry warned the US it would retaliate for any strike.
Tehran says the strait stays closed until seven conditions based on the Islamabad Memorandum are met. They include ending US 'acts of aggression', lifting the US naval blockade and releasing Iranian assets.
In the south, the Houthis, who are allied with Iran, have fired at Saudi Arabia repeatedly. Saudi forces intercepted missiles, one aimed at the Yanbu export terminal, though an Aramco administrative building in Dhahran was hit on Tuesday. The Houthis have declared a maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia.
Qatar is acting as a back channel, and mediators including Pakistan have earlier proposed a 10-day ceasefire.
levels.why: It puts a key oil route and Saudi exports at risk, which could keep energy costs high.

levels.headline: Attacks on ships and Saudi sites grow as Iran sets conditions for peace
levels.body:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards, a powerful military force, said sea mines stopped three tankers and set two on fire. At least nine ships have been attacked since Sunday. Iran is trying to block oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route. Its foreign ministry warned the US it would hit back if attacked.
Tehran says the strait will not reopen until the US meets seven conditions. They include ending what Iran calls acts of aggression, lifting the US naval blockade and releasing Iranian assets.
The Houthis, an Iran-backed group in Yemen, have fired at Saudi Arabia many times this week. Saudi forces shot down missiles, but an Aramco office building was hit on Tuesday. The Houthis have also said they will block Saudi shipping.
Qatar is passing messages between the sides, and Qatar and Pakistan earlier suggested a 10-day ceasefire.
levels.why: The fighting could keep oil dear and unsettle the region.

levels.headline: Iran and its allies attack ships and Saudi Arabia while peace talks stay stuck
levels.body:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards, a powerful part of its armed forces, say sea mines stopped three tankers and set two on fire. At least nine ships have been attacked since Sunday. Iran wants to stop oil leaving the Gulf through a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. It has warned the US that it will hit back if it is attacked.
Iran says the route will stay closed until the US agrees to seven demands. They include ending its attacks, lifting the US blockade, which keeps ships from entering Iranian ports, and releasing Iranian money held abroad.
The Houthis, a group in Yemen that backs Iran, have fired at Saudi Arabia this week. An Aramco office was hit. They also say they will block Saudi shipping.
Qatar is carrying messages between the sides.
levels.why: If oil can't flow freely, fuel and energy cost more around the world.

levels.headline: Ships and oil sites are attacked in the Middle East as peace talks stall

There is a war involving Iran in the Middle East, and it is getting worse. Iran's army group, the Revolutionary Guards, says sea mines stopped three oil ships and set two on fire. Qatar is trying to help the two sides talk.
levels.why: This affects oil prices, which touch the price of fuel and food everywhere.

levels.headline: The war with Iran grows as ships and Saudi oil sites are attacked

levels.why: When oil can't move freely, prices rise for petrol and many other things.

levels.headline: There is a war in the Middle East, and ships are being attacked

levels.why: Ships carry oil everywhere, so a war at sea can make petrol cost more.

levels.headline: Ships are being attacked in a war in the Middle East

One country in the war, Iran, wants to stop the ships passing through a narrow stretch of sea. It says it will let them through only if another country, the United States, agrees to seven things. They are like rules in a game that both sides must agree to.
Another group is firing rockets at a country called Saudi Arabia. An oil office was hit.
A small country called Qatar is helping everyone talk. Everyone hopes for peace.
levels.why: Oil ships carry fuel to many countries, so fighting at sea can make fuel cost more.

levels.headline: Trouble in France, and a rule to keep people indoors at night

In France, many people are upset. They are worried about schools and how much things cost. Last weekend, some of them smashed shops and took things. That is wrong. About 2,400 people were arrested. Some police and firefighters were hurt.
The Prime Minister, Sébastien Lecornu, has made a new rule in some places. It says people must stay indoors at night. It is called a curfew. It is meant to keep people safe. On Saturday there will be lots of police, and soldiers will help.
The President, Emmanuel Macron, is away on a trip to talk about fuel prices. Some people think he should be at home.
levels.why: It matters because broken shops mean lost work and things people need.

levels.headline: Fighting at sea in a faraway place

In a faraway part of the world there is a war. This week, big ships that carry oil were attacked at sea. Oil is used to make petrol for cars, so the ships are important to lots of people.

levels.why: Fighting at sea can make petrol and other things cost more for families.

headline: France keeps curfews and plans a military-backed security operation as Macron faces criticism over Gulf tour

levels.headline: France keeps curfews and plans a military-backed security operation as Macron faces criticism over Gulf tour
levels.body:
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said on Tuesday that some areas of France would stay under curfew after a weekend of violent rioting, and that new curfews would be imposed where the situation requires it, decided by prefects with mayors. Partial curfews were already in place in Paris, Bordeaux and Nice, and Lille and Nice have curfews for minors.
The government is planning a 'massive' security operation for Saturday, with military support, ahead of more planned protests. The unrest followed weeks of demonstrations over the education system, the cost of living and other issues. Police said hundreds of police officers, gendarmes and firefighters were injured and about 2,400 people arrested. At least 3,000 shops have reportedly been vandalised or looted.
President Emmanuel Macron is on a three-day Middle East tour, which he says aims to address high fuel prices and secure energy supplies. Critics say he should be at home. Jordan Bardella of the National Rally said the government is 'collapsing under its own weight'. Lecornu credited the curfews with a calmer night.
levels.why: The unrest tests the French government and could affect businesses, politics and stability in Europe.

levels.headline: French government extends curfews and plans military support after riots
levels.body:
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said some areas would remain under curfew after a weekend of violent rioting. He said more curfews would be imposed wherever needed, with prefects deciding in coordination with mayors. The unrest followed weeks of demonstrations about education, the cost of living and other concerns. Hundreds of officers and firefighters were injured, about 2,400 people were arrested, and at least 3,000 shops have been reported vandalised or looted.
President Emmanuel Macron is touring the Middle East for three days to discuss fuel prices and energy supplies, which has drawn criticism. National Rally's Jordan Bardella says the government is 'collapsing under its own weight'. The prime minister said the curfews helped bring a calmer night.
levels.why: It shows how cost-of-living anger can turn into unrest and put a government under pressure.

levels.headline: France keeps curfews after riots as the president's trip abroad draws criticism
levels.body:
France's Prime Minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said some areas will stay under curfew after a weekend of violent riots. A curfew is a rule that people must stay indoors at certain hours. levels.headline: Curfews stay in parts of France after the worst riots in years

France has had its worst riots for many years. The Prime Minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said some areas will keep a curfew. That is a rule that people must stay inside at set times. Local officials will add more curfews where they are needed. Paris, Bordeaux and Nice already have some.

levels.headline: France keeps night-time curfews after days of riots

Many people in France have been protesting about schools, the high cost of living and other problems. Over the weekend some protests turned into riots. Shops were smashed and robbed. About 2,400 people have been arrested. Many police officers and firefighters were hurt.

levels.headline: France uses curfews to calm riots, and the president is away

levels.headline: France tries to calm riots with night-time rules

levels.why: It matters because riots hurt shops and workers and show how worried people are about money.

levels.why: It matters because when people are upset about money, shops and workers can get hurt.

levels.headline: The US president wants Ukraine to make a deal with Russia

There is a war in Ukraine. Russia began it. The United States has been helping Ukraine. On Tuesday, the US president, Donald Trump, said it is time to make a deal to end the war. He said the US had not got much back for helping.
He said this after Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, met American helpers in a city called Oslo. Mr Trump said that helping costs a lot and many Americans are tired of it.
Mr Zelenskyy said he had a good phone call with an American leader, Marco Rubio. He would like a big meeting with Mr Trump and Russia's president, Mr Putin. An American helper will go to Russia on Wednesday.
levels.why: A deal could end the fighting, so it matters a great deal to people in Ukraine.

levels.headline: There has been trouble in France, and a rule keeps people indoors at night

Imagine a playground where many children are upset. They are cross about their school and about how much things cost. Some of them started breaking things. That is not allowed, and grown-ups had to step in.
In France, this happened for real. Some people smashed shops last weekend. The helper of the country's leader, called the Prime Minister, made a rule in some places. People must stay indoors at night. It keeps everyone safe while things calm down. On Saturday there will be lots of police, and soldiers will help.
The main leader, the President, is away on a trip. Some people think he should be at home.
levels.why: It matters because broken shops mean people lose work and things they need.

headline: 'Time to make a deal,' Trump tells Zelenskyy, complaining the US has got 'nothing back' from Ukraine

levels.headline: 'Time to make a deal,' Trump tells Zelenskyy, complaining the US has got 'nothing back' from Ukraine
levels.body:
US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday 20 October that it was 'time to make a deal' with Russia, telling Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy that the US has got 'nothing back' from Ukraine. He spoke to reporters at the White House shortly after Mr Zelenskyy met a US delegation led by special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo.
Mr Trump said Mr Zelenskyy could have made a deal two years ago and that Ukraine's leaders may not tolerate the situation much longer. He described US support as costly and said the American public is tired of it. Euronews also reports that he said it was 'time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine'.
The Oslo talks also included Finland's President Stubb and Norway's Prime Minister Støre. Afterwards Mr Zelenskyy said he had held a constructive call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and called for a trilateral meeting with Mr Trump and Russia's President Putin. Mr Witkoff was due to travel to Russia on Wednesday to meet Mr Putin.
levels.why: US support is central to Ukraine's defence, and pressure to settle could shape the war and Europe's security.

levels.headline: Trump presses Zelenskyy to do a deal with Russia and says the US has got 'nothing back'
levels.body:
Donald Trump told Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Tuesday it was 'time to make a deal', saying the US has had 'nothing back' from Ukraine. He spoke at the White House soon after Mr Zelenskyy met a US team led by special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo.
Mr Trump said Mr Zelenskyy could have reached a deal two years ago and that Ukraine's leaders may not put up with the situation much longer. He called US support expensive and said Americans are tired of it. He also said it was time for somebody else to negotiate for Ukraine, according to Euronews.
Finland's President Stubb and Norway's Prime Minister Støre also took part in the Oslo talks. Mr Zelenskyy said he had a constructive call with Secretary of State Marco Rubio and asked for a three-way meeting with Mr Trump and Vladimir Putin. Mr Witkoff is due to meet Mr Putin in Russia on Wednesday.
levels.why: The US is Ukraine's key backer, so shifts in its stance can change the course of the war.

levels.headline: Trump tells Ukraine's president it is 'time to make a deal'
levels.body:
US President Donald Trump said it was 'time to make a deal' with Russia as he spoke about Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, on Tuesday. He said the US had got 'nothing back' from Ukraine for its support. He was talking at the White House just after Mr Zelenskyy met a US team in Oslo, led by Steve Witkoff, a special envoy, which means someone sent to deal with a specific issue.
Mr Trump said Mr Zelenskyy could have made a deal two years ago. He said US help was costly and Americans were tired of it. He also said it was time for somebody else to negotiate for Ukraine.
Leaders from Finland and Norway joined the Oslo talks. Mr Zelenskyy said he had a good call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and wants a meeting of Mr Trump, himself and Russia's President Putin. Mr Witkoff is due to meet Mr Putin on Wednesday.
levels.why: What the US decides could affect how long the war lasts and how safe Europe feels.

levels.headline: Trump says it is 'time to make a deal' as he presses Ukraine to end the war
levels.body:
US President Donald Trump has told Ukraine's leader, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, that it is 'time to make a deal' to end the war with Russia. He said the US had got 'nothing back' for its help. He said this on Tuesday, soon after Mr Zelenskyy met American officials in Oslo, the capital of Norway. They were led by Steve Witkoff, a special envoy, who is someone sent to deal with one particular issue.
Mr Trump said Mr Zelenskyy could have made a deal two years ago. He said helping Ukraine costs a lot and that Americans are tired of it. He also said somebody else should do the talking for Ukraine.
Mr Zelenskyy said he had a helpful call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. He wants a meeting of himself, Mr Trump and Russia's President Putin. Mr Witkoff is due to go to Russia on Wednesday.
levels.why: If US help changes, it could change how the war goes and how safe Europe is.

levels.headline: Trump tells Ukraine's leader it is time to agree a deal with Russia
levels.body:
Russia invaded Ukraine, and the war is still going on. The United States has helped Ukraine. On Tuesday, US President Donald Trump said it was 'time to make a deal' to end it. He said the US had got 'nothing back' for its help. He said this just after Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, met American officials in Oslo, in Norway. A man called Steve Witkoff led the American team.
Mr Trump said helping Ukraine costs a lot and that Americans are tired of it. He also said Mr Zelenskyy could have made a deal two years ago.
Mr Zelenskyy said he had a good phone call with another US leader, Marco Rubio. He wants a meeting with Mr Trump and Russia's President Putin. Mr Witkoff will go to Russia on Wednesday.
levels.why: The decisions of big countries can decide how long a war lasts.

levels.headline: Trump says Ukraine should make a deal with Russia
levels.body:
Russia invaded Ukraine, and the war is still going on. The United States has been helping Ukraine. On Tuesday, the US president, Donald Trump, said it was time for a deal to end the war. He said the US had got nothing back for its help. He said this after Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, met American officials in Oslo, in Norway.
Mr Trump said helping Ukraine costs a lot of money, and that Americans are tired of it. He also said Mr Zelenskyy could have made a deal two years ago.
Mr Zelenskyy said he had a good phone call with an American leader called Marco Rubio. He wants a meeting with Mr Trump and Russia's president, Mr Putin. An American helper, Steve Witkoff, will go to Russia on Wednesday.
levels.why: If the help stops, the war could change, and that matters for people across Europe.

levels.headline: The US president wants Ukraine to make a deal
levels.body:
There is a war in a country called Ukraine. Another country, Russia, started it. The United States has been helping Ukraine. On Tuesday, the US president, Donald Trump, said it is time to make a deal to end the war. He said the US has not got much back for helping.
He said this after Ukraine's leader, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, met some American helpers in a city called Oslo.
Mr Trump said that helping costs a lot of money and that many Americans are tired of it. Mr Zelenskyy said he had a good talk with another American leader. He would like a big meeting with Mr Trump and the Russian leader, Mr Putin. An American helper will go to Russia on Wednesday.
levels.why: A deal could end the war, but the terms matter a lot to people in Ukraine.

levels.headline: Leaders talk about how to end a war
levels.body:
There is a war in a country called Ukraine. Another country, Russia, began it. A big country called the United States has been helping Ukraine. This week the leader of the United States said it is time to make a deal, which means to agree to stop the fighting.
He said that helping costs a lot of money and that many people in his country are tired of paying. He also said his country had not got much back for helping.
Ukraine's leader met some helpers from the United States in a city called Oslo. He said it was a good talk. Next, a helper will visit Russia to talk to its leader.
Everyone hopes the fighting will stop soon.
levels.why: A deal could end the fighting, so what the leaders decide matters to many people.

levels.headline: People in Alberta choose to stay in Canada
levels.body:
Canada is a very big country made of parts called provinces. One is called Alberta. Last Monday, people in Alberta voted. They were asked a question about leaving Canada. Most said they wanted to stay. About three in every four did.
Some people in Alberta want it to be its own country. They hoped to win and have another vote. They did not win this time.
The leader of Canada, Mark Carney, said the people of Alberta chose Canada. The leader of Alberta, Danielle Smith, said there will be no more votes about leaving while she is in charge. Those who want to leave say they will keep trying.
levels.why: It shows how people feel about staying together as one country.

levels.headline: Grown-ups try to stop a fight between countries
levels.body:
Two countries are fighting. Russia began it. Ukraine has been defending itself. A big friend, the United States, has helped Ukraine. This week the leader of the big friend said it is time to make a deal. A deal means both sides agree to stop.
The leader said that helping costs a lot and that many people in his country are tired of paying. It is a bit like a friend who says, 'I have helped a lot, now please sort this out.'
Ukraine's leader met some helpers from the big friend. He said it was a good talk. Next, a helper will go to Russia to talk to its leader.
Everyone hopes the fighting will stop soon.
levels.why: A deal could mean children in Ukraine can feel safe again.

headline: Alberta votes by a large majority to stay in Canada, giving Prime Minister Carney a boost

terms.meaning: A public vote on one question.
Not legally forcing the government to act on the result.
Someone who wants a region to break away and become independent.

levels.headline: Alberta votes by a large majority to stay in Canada, giving Prime Minister Carney a boost
levels.body:
Voters in the Canadian province of Alberta rejected separation in a non-binding referendum held on Monday 19 October. Early counts showed about three in four backing 'remain'. CNBC reported 76% for remain against 24% with three-quarters of votes counted, and Elections Alberta's unofficial tally of more than a million votes had 77% backing staying in Canada.
The vote was not a direct ballot on independence. A win for the separatists would have set the province on a path towards a binding referendum on leaving. Provisional results showed voters backed eight of the nine questions put to them, some by small majorities.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Albertans chose Canada, and Premier Danielle Smith promised not to call another separation referendum while she is premier. Separatist Jeffrey Rath said the movement would carry on, aiming to take control of the United Conservative Party, while organiser David Parker conceded that independence 'feels far away'. The figures are unofficial, so final numbers may differ slightly.
levels.why: The result eases fears about Canada splitting and shows how regional and national politics can clash.

levels.headline: Alberta rejects separation in a referendum, and separatists vow to continue
levels.body:
Alberta voted by a wide margin to remain part of Canada in a non-binding referendum on Monday 19 October. Early counts put support for remaining at about three-quarters. CNBC reported 76% to 24% with three-quarters of votes counted, and an unofficial Elections Alberta tally of over a million votes had 77% for staying.
The question was not a direct vote on independence. Had the separatists won, it would have started a path towards a binding referendum on leaving Canada. Provisional results showed voters backed eight of the nine questions, some narrowly.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Albertans chose Canada. Premier Danielle Smith promised not to call another separation referendum while she is premier. Separatist Jeffrey Rath said the movement would try to take control of the United Conservative Party, and David Parker said it was a defeat. These are unofficial counts, so final numbers may change slightly.
levels.why: It strengthens national unity for now, but the separatist movement says it is not going away.

levels.headline: Albertans vote to stay in Canada
levels.body:
People in Alberta, a province in western Canada, voted on Monday 19 October on a question about leaving Canada. The vote was non-binding, which means the government did not have to act on the result. About three in four voters wanted to remain. CNBC reported 76% to 24% with three-quarters of votes counted, and another early count had 77% for staying.
The vote was not a direct choice about independence. If the separatists had won, the province would have moved towards a binding vote on leaving. Voters backed eight of the nine questions on the ballot, some by small margins.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Albertans chose Canada. Premier Danielle Smith said she would not call another vote on separation while she is premier. Separatists said they will keep going and try to take over the governing party, but one organiser admitted it was a defeat. These numbers are early and unofficial.
levels.why: It tells us how united Canada feels, and it is a boost for the prime minister.

levels.headline: Alberta votes to remain part of Canada, but separatists say they will keep trying
levels.body:
Alberta is a large province in western Canada. On Monday 19 October its people voted in a referendum, which is a public vote on a question. This one was non-binding, so the government did not have to follow the result. About three in four voters wanted to stay in Canada. Early counts showed 76% to 77% for staying.
The vote was not directly about independence. If the separatists had won, it would have started a path towards a second, binding vote on leaving. Voters also backed eight of nine other questions on the ballot.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Albertans chose Canada. The head of the province, Danielle Smith, said there will be no more votes on leaving while she is in charge. Separatists, who want Alberta to leave, said they would keep fighting but one admitted it was a defeat. The numbers are early.
levels.why: It shows that most people in Alberta want to stay in Canada, for now.

levels.headline: Alberta says no to leaving Canada
levels.body:
Alberta is a big province in the west of Canada. On Monday 19 October, people there voted on a question about leaving Canada. The vote was non-binding. That means the government did not have to do what the vote said. About three in every four people wanted to stay. The early count was 76% for staying and 24% against.
The question was not exactly about leaving. If the people who want to leave had won, the next step would have been another, stronger vote. Voters also said yes to eight other questions.
The Prime Minister, Mark Carney, said people in Alberta chose Canada. The Premier, Danielle Smith, said she would not call another vote while she is in charge. Those who want to leave say they will keep trying. The numbers are early and may change a little.
levels.why: It shows whether people in a part of the country feel part of the whole country.

Canada is a very big country, made of parts called provinces. One of them is called Alberta. On Monday 19 October, people in Alberta voted on a question about leaving Canada. The vote could not force the government to do anything. About three in four people said they wanted to stay.

The Prime Minister of Canada, Mark Carney, said Albertans chose Canada. The leader of Alberta, Danielle Smith, said there will be no new votes on leaving while she is in charge. The people who want to leave say they will keep trying. The numbers are early and may change a little.
levels.why: It shows how a country's people feel about staying together.

levels.headline: Alberta votes to stay part of Canada
