Some people in Alberta want it to be its own country. They hoped to win and have another vote. They did not win this time.
The leader of Canada, Mark Carney, said the people of Alberta chose Canada. The leader of Alberta, Danielle Smith, said there will be no more votes about leaving while she is in charge. The people who want to leave say they will keep trying.
levels.why: It matters because it shows how people feel about their country.

levels.headline: The people of Alberta choose to stay in Canada
levels.body:
Canada is a huge country with different parts. One part is called Alberta. Last Monday, the people who live in Alberta voted. Voting means everyone gets to say what they think. They were asked about leaving Canada. Most said no. About three in every four said they wanted to stay.
Some people in Alberta want it to be its own country. They did not get enough votes this time.
The leader of Canada said people chose to stay together. The leader of Alberta said there will be no more votes on leaving while she is in charge. Those who want to leave say they will keep trying.
In a democracy, people can say what they want, and then the votes are counted.
levels.why: Voting lets people have a say in how their country is run.

levels.headline: Britain thinks about taxing cars from China
levels.body:
Many people in Britain are buying electric cars made in China. When goods come from another country, the government can add a tax. This is called a tariff. Britain's tariff is small, just 10%. The countries next door in the EU have a much bigger one, up to 35.3%.
The EU wants to protect the cars it makes. Some think Britain should do the same. A newspaper said a minister is thinking about it. The government says it has not decided.
It is a tricky choice. The Prime Minister wants Britain to be friends with the EU. But China does not want the tax. Cars with a battery and an engine would still pay no extra.
levels.why: A tax could make cars cost more and upset another country.

levels.headline: A big vote in a part of Canada
levels.body:
Imagine your class is part of a big school. One day, some children ask, 'Should our class leave the school and be on its own?' Everyone gets to vote. Most children say, 'No, let's stay.' About three in every four say that.
Something like this happened in a place called Alberta, which is part of the country Canada. Last Monday, people there voted on whether to leave. Most wanted to stay. A few still want to leave, and they say they will try again.
The leaders said they were happy that most people chose to stay together.
Voting is a fair way for people to decide big things.
levels.why: Voting is a fair way to decide big things together.

headline: Britain welcomed Chinese electric cars and now faces a difficult choice over tariffs

terms.meaning: A tax charged on goods brought into a country.
A car with a battery that can be charged from a socket, plus a petrol or diesel engine.
EU plans to favour products made in Europe.

levels.headline: Britain welcomed Chinese electric cars and now faces a difficult choice over tariffs
levels.body:
Britain has no China-specific tariffs on electric vehicles, so Chinese-built cars face only the standard 10% import duty. That makes it one of the largest major overseas markets without extra levies. The EU, by contrast, applies company-by-company duties on Chinese electric vehicles of up to 35.3%.
CNBC reports that EU proposals could push London to match those levies, partly to avoid being caught by the EU's 'Made in Europe' rules. The Sunday Times reported that a UK minister was considering matching the EU duty. A government spokesperson said it had not imposed tariffs and was still engaging with industry. An ING economist argued that the gap between Britain and the EU leaves the UK with limited options besides tariffs.
The choice is finely balanced given Prime Minister Andy Burnham's wish to reset relations with the EU, and China's embassy has said it firmly opposes tariff rises. Analysts note that Britain also charges no extra tariff on plug-in hybrids, so tariffs on battery cars alone would not stop Chinese brands' rapid growth.
levels.why: The decision affects car prices, trade with China and the UK's room to move closer to the EU.

levels.headline: Britain faces a tariff dilemma as Chinese electric cars gain ground
levels.body:
Chinese electric cars have flooded into Britain, which charges only the standard 10% import duty on them. The EU charges up to 35.3% on Chinese electric vehicles, with a different rate for each manufacturer.
CNBC says EU plans could push Britain to copy those tariffs, in part to avoid the EU's 'Made in Europe' rules. The Sunday Times reported that a UK minister was considering matching the EU duty. The government says it has imposed no tariffs and is talking to industry. An ING economist says Britain has few other options as its policies drift away from the EU's.
There are trade-offs. Prime Minister Andy Burnham wants closer relations with the EU, but China's embassy says it firmly opposes higher tariffs. Analysts also point out that Britain charges no extra tariff on plug-in hybrids, so a tariff on fully electric cars alone would only slow part of the Chinese expansion.
levels.why: It could change what UK drivers pay for new cars and how Britain balances China and the EU.

levels.headline: Britain must decide whether to put tariffs on Chinese electric cars
levels.body:
Britain has become one of the easiest big markets for Chinese electric cars, because it charges only the standard 10% import tax on them. The European Union charges much more, up to 35.3% depending on the maker.
CNBC reports that the EU's plans could push Britain to do the same, partly so UK firms are not shut out by the EU's 'Made in Europe' rules. The Sunday Times said a UK minister was thinking about copying the EU's tax. The government says it has not added any tariffs yet and is still talking to carmakers. An economist at ING says Britain has few other choices.
It is a tricky decision. Prime Minister Andy Burnham wants to be closer to the EU. China has said it strongly opposes tax rises. Plug-in hybrid cars have no extra tax in Britain either, so Chinese firms could keep growing.
levels.why: Car prices, jobs and Britain's relations with both China and Europe could all be affected.

levels.headline: Should Britain tax Chinese electric cars? The government has a hard choice
levels.body:
Many people in Britain are buying electric cars made by Chinese companies. Britain charges only a normal import tax of 10% on them. This kind of tax on goods from abroad is called a tariff. The European Union charges more, up to 35.3%, depending on the company.
Now the EU has plans that could push Britain to do the same. One reason is a set of EU rules called 'Made in Europe'. A newspaper reported that a UK minister was thinking about matching the EU's tax. The government says it has not added any tax and is still talking to the industry.
There are good reasons on each side. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, wants better links with the EU. China says it does not want higher taxes. Also, cars that use both a battery and fuel have no extra tax, so Chinese firms may keep growing anyway.
levels.why: The choice could change car prices and affect trade with both China and Europe.

levels.headline: Britain is deciding whether to add taxes on electric cars made in China
levels.body:
Lots of electric cars made in China are now sold in Britain. When goods come into a country from abroad, the country can charge a tax on them. This is called a tariff. Britain charges only 10% on Chinese electric cars. The European Union charges more, up to 35.3%.
Some people think Britain may need to copy the EU. This is partly because of EU rules called 'Made in Europe', which could make life harder for British firms. A newspaper said a minister was thinking about it. The government says it has not added a tax and is still talking with car companies.
It is a hard choice. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, wants to get closer to the EU. But China says it does not want higher taxes. Also, cars with both a battery and an engine would still have no extra tax.
levels.why: A tax on these cars could make them cost more, and might upset China.

levels.headline: Britain must choose whether to put extra taxes on Chinese electric cars
levels.body:
More and more cars sold in Britain are electric cars from China. When a country lets in goods from abroad, it can charge a tax on them. This is called a tariff. Britain charges 10% on these cars. The European Union, which is the group of countries next door, charges up to 35.3%.
The EU wants to protect its own car makers. Some think Britain should do the same, so that British car makers are not left out. A newspaper said a minister was thinking about it. The government says it has not decided.
It is a hard choice. The Prime Minister wants to be closer to the EU. China does not want the tax. And cars with a battery plus an engine would stay tax-free, so Chinese car firms could keep growing.
levels.why: It could change how much cars cost and how Britain gets on with other countries.

levels.headline: Should Britain tax electric cars from China?
levels.body:
Many people in Britain are buying electric cars made in China. When goods come from another country, the government can add a tax. This is called a tariff. Britain adds a small one, 10%. The countries next door in the EU add a much bigger one, up to 35.3%.
The EU wants to protect the cars it makes. Some people think Britain should do the same. A newspaper said a minister is thinking about it, but the government says it has not decided yet.
It is not an easy choice. The Prime Minister wants Britain to be better friends with the EU. But China does not want the tax, and it has said so. Also, a car with a battery and an engine would still have no extra tax, so Chinese car makers might keep selling lots of cars.
levels.why: A tax could make cars cost more, and it might upset another country.

levels.headline: Should Britain add a tax to cars from China?
levels.body:
Many families in Britain now drive electric cars that were built in China. When something is brought into a country, the government can add a tax. This is called a tariff. It is like a small fee at the border. Britain's fee is small. The fee in the countries next door is much bigger.
The neighbours want to protect the cars they make. Some people think Britain should do the same. A newspaper said a minister is thinking about it. The government says it has not decided yet.
It is a tricky choice. The Prime Minister wants Britain to be friends with the neighbours. But China does not like the fee and has said so. And some cars have a battery and an engine, and they would still pay no extra.
levels.why: A fee could make cars cost more, and could make another country unhappy.

levels.headline: Oil is dearer because of fighting far away
levels.body:
Oil is a thick black liquid from under the ground. We use it to make petrol for cars. Oil is sold in barrels. A barrel costs about $109 now. That is the most since May. A year ago it cost much less.
Why? There is fighting in the Middle East. Ships carrying oil have been attacked. Places that make oil in Saudi Arabia have been attacked too. When people fear there will not be enough oil, they pay more to get it.
Some people say there may be a new peace plan, but nobody has said it is real.
When oil costs more, petrol, heating and food can cost more too.
levels.why: Oil costs touch lots of everyday things, so families notice when it rises.

levels.headline: Should Britain charge a fee on cars from China?
levels.body:
Imagine a school fair where children sell things. Now some children from another school bring really good toy cars, and everyone wants to buy them. Your school can say, 'You must pay a small fee to sell here.' That fee is like a tariff, which is a tax on things from abroad.
Britain only charges a small fee for electric cars from China. The countries next door charge a much bigger fee. Some people think Britain should copy them. The government has not decided.
It is tricky. The Prime Minister wants to be friends with the neighbours. But China would not like a bigger fee, and it has said so.
Whatever happens, grown-ups will keep thinking about it carefully.
levels.why: A fee might make toy cars, and real cars, cost more.

headline: US borrowing costs stay near multi-decade highs as markets expect the Fed to hold rates in October

terms.meaning: The return investors get from lending to the US government, which moves opposite to bond prices.
The central bank of the United States, which sets its main interest rate.
The rate at which prices rise over time.

levels.headline: US borrowing costs stay near multi-decade highs as markets expect the Fed to hold rates in October
levels.body:
The 10-year US Treasury yield was about 5.12% on 20 October, after Treasury yields hit a 24-year high on 19 October. In September the Federal Reserve raised its benchmark range to 3.75% to 4%, from 3.5% to 3.75%, its first hike in three years.
Traders now put the chance of the Fed leaving rates unchanged at its 28 October meeting above 80%, according to CME FedWatch as of 19 October, though odds of a hike have swung between about 15% and 35% in recent days. More than 90% of traders see at least one more hike before the end of the year, according to a 14 October report.
Inflation is a concern. Consumer prices were up 3.7% on a year earlier in September, beating estimates, and wholesale prices rose 6.3%, the biggest jump since 2022. Fed minutes say officials attribute rising yields to expected rate rises, the build-out in artificial intelligence and solid growth.
levels.why: US interest rates and bond yields influence mortgage costs, share prices and borrowing worldwide.

levels.headline: Treasury yields stay high and traders expect the Fed to hold, then hike later
levels.body:
The 10-year US Treasury yield was around 5.12% on 20 October. Treasury yields reached a 24-year high the day before. In September the Federal Reserve raised its key rate range to 3.75% to 4%, its first increase in three years.
CME FedWatch data on 19 October showed more than an 80% chance the Fed holds rates at its 28 October meeting, although the odds of a rise have moved between about 15% and 35% in a week. A December hike is widely expected, with over 90% odds of at least one more rise this year as of 14 October.
Inflation remains a worry. Consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year to September, above forecasts, and wholesale prices were up 6.3%, the largest rise since 2022. Fed officials attribute higher yields to expected rate rises, heavy AI investment and solid growth.
levels.why: Because US yields set a benchmark for global borrowing, they affect UK and European costs too.

levels.headline: US borrowing costs stay high, with the Fed expected to wait before raising rates again
levels.body:
The interest rate on a 10-year loan to the US government, called the Treasury yield, was about 5.12% on 20 October. A day earlier it hit its highest level in 24 years. In September the Federal Reserve, America's central bank, raised its main interest rate range to 3.75% to 4%. It was the first rise in three years.
Traders think the Fed will leave rates unchanged at its next meeting on 28 October, with the chance at over 80%. But more than nine in ten expect at least one more rise by the end of the year.
One reason is inflation. Prices were 3.7% higher in September than a year before, more than expected. Wholesale prices rose 6.3%. Fed officials say yields are high because of expected rate rises, spending on artificial intelligence and solid growth.
levels.why: When the US government pays more to borrow, it pushes up borrowing costs for many others.

levels.headline: Borrowing costs in the US stay high as the Fed prepares for its next meeting
levels.body:
When a government borrows money, it pays interest. In the US, the interest rate on a 10-year loan to the government, called the Treasury yield, was about 5.12% on 20 October. A day earlier it reached its highest in 24 years.
In September, the Federal Reserve, which is America's central bank, raised its main rate to a range of 3.75% to 4%. It was the first rise in three years. Most traders think the Fed will keep rates the same at its next meeting on 28 October, but most also think it will raise them again before the end of the year.
The reason is inflation, meaning prices rising. Prices were 3.7% higher in September than a year before. That was more than people had expected.
Fed officials say yields have risen because of rate expectations, AI spending and solid growth.
levels.why: Higher rates make loans and mortgages dearer and can slow the economy.

levels.headline: US interest rates are high and may rise again
levels.body:
The government of the United States borrows money by selling bonds. The interest it pays on a 10-year bond is called the Treasury yield. It is about 5.12%, which is high. Last week it reached its highest in 24 years.
The United States has a central bank called the Federal Reserve. It sets the country's main interest rate. In September it raised the rate to between 3.75% and 4%. That was the first rise in three years. Most traders think it will leave the rate alone at its meeting on 28 October. But many think it will raise it again before the end of the year.
The worry is inflation. Prices went up 3.7% in the year to September. That was more than experts expected.
levels.why: US rates affect borrowing costs around the world, including loans and mortgages.

levels.headline: Borrowing costs in the US are high, and may go higher
levels.body:
Governments borrow money, just like families do. The US government pays interest on what it borrows. For loans of ten years, that interest is now about 5.12% a year. That is very high. Last week it was the highest in 24 years.
The US also has a central bank, called the Federal Reserve. It sets the main interest rate for the country. In September, it raised the rate. It was the first rise in three years. Most people who trade bonds think it will keep the rate the same at its next meeting on 28 October. They think it will raise the rate again before the year ends.
The worry is inflation, which means prices going up. Prices in the US were 3.7% higher in September than a year before.
levels.why: Higher rates make loans cost more and can slow things down.

levels.headline: The cost of borrowing is high in America
levels.body:
If you borrow money, you usually pay a bit extra. That extra is called interest. The government of the United States borrows money too, and it now pays high interest. For loans lasting ten years, it pays about 5.12% a year. That is the most for 24 years.
The country has a central bank, called the Federal Reserve. It decides the main interest rate. In September it made the rate higher, for the first time in three years. People think it will wait at its next meeting on 28 October. But many think it will make the rate higher again before the end of the year.
The reason is that prices are going up. In September, prices were 3.7% higher than a year before.
levels.why: When borrowing costs more, families and firms may spend less.

levels.headline: Borrowing money costs a lot in America
levels.body:
When you borrow money, you pay back a little extra. That extra is called interest. The government of America borrows money too. It now pays a lot of extra. It pays about 5 pence for every 100 pence it borrows each year. That is the most for 24 years.
A big bank, called the Federal Reserve, decides how much extra people pay across the country. In September it made the extra bigger. Many people think it will wait before changing it again. But they think it will raise it again before the end of the year.
The reason is that prices are going up. A sweet that cost 100 pence last year now costs about 104 pence.
levels.why: When borrowing costs more, families may have less money to spend.

levels.headline: Borrowing money is getting more expensive in America
levels.body:
If you borrow a toy from a friend, you might promise to give back a small treat as a thank you. When grown-ups borrow money, they pay back a little extra too. That extra is called interest.
In America, borrowing money has become very expensive. The government has to pay a lot of extra when it borrows. A big bank, called the Federal Reserve, helps decide how much extra everyone pays. It made the extra bigger in September.
Some grown-ups think it will stay the same for a while. Many think it will go up again before the end of the year.
The reason is that prices are rising. A sweet that cost 100 pence last year now costs a bit more.
levels.why: When borrowing costs more, families and shops may have less to spend.
